utterances.speaker: Here we have in front of us a decision from
utterances.text: "Serbs" mean a people. They were a people. In this conflict, we cannot condemn any people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fair enough. Was the Bosnian Serb --

utterances.speaker: Here we have in front of us a decision from
utterances.text: They were members of the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And it was the Bosnian Serb army that was the embodiment of this particular enemy? Would you say that's a fair classification?

utterances.speaker: Here we have in front of us a decision from
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you left Kakanj, what was your route?

utterances.speaker: Here we have in front of us a decision from
utterances.text: I went through the woods. I did not use roads. There were no roads in many areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you get to your next place of -- your next destination, which was what? Where were you actually headed? What was your goal to get to at the time?

utterances.speaker: Here we have in front of us a decision from
utterances.text: If you want to know about the populated areas, that was Poljanice, which was predominantly inhabited by Croats, the village of Lucici--

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. That wasn't the question. Where were you headed for? You were leaving Kakanj for where? What was your destination?

utterances.speaker: Here we have in front of us a decision from
utterances.text: Vares.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is Anto Pejcinovic? Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: Here we have in front of us a decision from
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would like to ask the usher, please, to distribute Exhibit Z1110. It is in both English and Croatian. I'm informed it was part of the outstanding exhibits. Therefore, it should be contained in the binder. But I would appreciate it being exhibited on the ELMO as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you have in front of you is a document signed by Anto Pejcinovic, and again can you please indicate how you know Pejcinovic?

utterances.speaker: Here we have in front of us a decision from
utterances.text: Pejcinovic was the president of the municipal assembly, that is, the Vares HVO. That was the only neighbouring municipality with which we had open communication lines, so I know him from those contacts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document, dated 25th of July, 1993, and signed by Anto Pejcinovic, reads: "For the attention of the army of the Republika Srpska." Now, is that the Bosnian Serb army we've just discussed?

utterances.speaker: Here we have in front of us a decision from
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you. He requests -- the request is to enable passage for refugees. It doesn't say "displaced persons", it says "refugees", and it says: "We are writing to you to request that you allow five of our buses carrying 335 refugees to leave the territory of Kakanj municipality and travel on the --" let's see. Is it --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Blagoje.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: " ... Kobiljaca road to Kiseljak in order to find accommodation. Please find enclosed a list of people who will be travelling on the buses. "We thank you in advance, hoping that you will meet our requirements and provide the required escort." And it is signed by Anto Pejcinovic as president of the HVO, Vares municipality, indeed a similar to the one you once held in Kakanj. Looking behind the document to the attachments in English on page -- well, it would end in "0388", but it is item number 112, and it should be listed as 112 in the Croatian as well. You are listed, you and your family are listed; is that correct? Do you recall -- I'm sorry, is that a "yes"?

utterances.speaker: Here we have in front of us a decision from
utterances.text: I don't recall exactly this list, but I know that all displaced persons from Vares crossed into Kiseljak through the territory controlled by the BSA en route to Herzegovina; Stolac, Capljina and other points. But if this refers to the same date, because I see that the attachment has been signed as a separate document, not as an enclosure to this document, I left Vares on 17 October 1993, again through the territory controlled by the BSA to the territory of Kiseljak, and I went there as a soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whether you initially were scheduled to go on this particular trip or another I think is probably not central to the point. The point is you not only crossed through Serb territory, Pejcinovic asked that you be escorted, escorted through Serb territory, territory which is, as you explained, enemy territory. Can you possibly explain how this came to be?

utterances.speaker: Here we have in front of us a decision from
utterances.text: The escort was asked and received. The buses passed through. We reached our destination. Now, how this was done, if I'm not interrupted, I could clarify in some detail. In Kakanj, there were about 8.000 Serbs. Croatian people and the HVO were never hostile towards this ethnic group because they felt that they were not a threat to the Croatian population of Kakanj. So by leaving them alone, the members of the Kakanj HVO still went to help out at the front line in Jajce, Teslic, and other areas where the territory of the current Federation was under an attack by the Bosnian Serb forces. Those members of the Serbian population who were armed, they were our enemy, and the others were regular, honest citizens, just like everyone else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that your explanation? Is that your explanation?

utterances.speaker: Here we have in front of us a decision from
utterances.text: So given that at one point the HVO protected this population which lived in seven or eight villages in the Kakanj municipality, probably as a counter-favour the leadership of the Republika Srpska allowed the Croatian population to pass through their territory, fleeing from the Bosnian Muslim forces. It may look as a paradox, but when a part of our troops arrived in the Stolac territory, they again joined in the battle against the forces of Bosnian Serbs. It may seem a little bit illogical, but this is how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivic, it does seem a paradox, I have to say. Again, the document is addressed not to those good Serbs who were living peacefully in your fair municipality but rather to the army of the Republika Srpska. Now, may I ask you, did you pay money to go across? Did you have to pay any kind of fee to get out of Kakanj, to get to your ultimate destination?

utterances.speaker: Here we have in front of us a decision from
utterances.text: When I left Kakanj, I was wearing a uniform, I carried a rifle, and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you deserted, you didn't flee?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. You were asked -- we will get on more quickly if you will just answer the question shortly. You were asked if you paid a fee, any money, to get out. Now, the answer to that is either "yes" or "no". Could you please tell us?

utterances.speaker: Here we have in front of us a decision from
utterances.text: "No".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In order to allow us to wind down your -- actually to complete your testimony on cross, you were in uniform and you were also, as I see from this list, whether they all left at this particular time or at a later time if you say you left in October, Blasko Pavlovic, your successor as president of the HVO, Franjo Maric, the deputy, I mean everybody left. Are you suggesting that the entire structure of a nascent -- of a beginning group of municipal formation of the HZ HB in Kakanj up and left just like that?

utterances.speaker: Here we have in front of us a decision from
utterances.text: Did not leave. I said that I left on the 17th of October. Here I see another date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did Mr. Maric and did Mr. Pavlovic also leave at some point?

utterances.speaker: Here we have in front of us a decision from
utterances.text: They left, and I believe that Mr. Pavlovic and Mr. Maric both went to Stolac, I think even one day earlier, so that would be on the 16th October 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the entire power structure of HZ HB, as represented by the HVO in Kakanj, left. It simply abandoned Kakanj; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Here we have in front of us a decision from
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The angst that was described earlier, which I think is evident in the document of 30 September 1992, suggests clearly, does it not, in your opinion, that it was not easy to remain exclusively Croat in such a geographic location? Do you agree with that? For Kakanj to remain exclusively Croat, it was difficult; is that true?

utterances.speaker: Here we have in front of us a decision from
utterances.text: That was impossible under any circumstances. That was a concept that I think is being forced on me now. That was not a reasonable or a logical or supported by any elements of our struggle for survival. Your Honours, let me say one more thing. You insisted I answer with a "yes" or "no". It is put to me that I left. I didn't leave. I had to flee, and I couldn't fly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You know, we are spending a great deal of time on complete irrelevancies.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The point that I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not criticising you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I wanted to make sure that the Court had in evidence the issue of an entire structure leaving, which I think will be very significant for final arguments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Can we wind this up, as you put it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know Dario Kordic, you know the thinkers, the politicians, the planners of Herceg-Bosna. Did it appear to you at any point that anything that Mr. Kordic did or didn't do could turn Kakanj into a purely Croat municipality that would satisfy the needs of membership in Herceg-Bosna? Did it ever seem a reality? Could he really remedy it, in your opinion? Please help us.

utterances.speaker: Here we have in front of us a decision from
utterances.text: I answered that question a couple of minutes ago. Anyone in that area, in that ethnic composition, if they advocated such an idea would not be able to implement it. If they would just -- by that they would sacrifice the entire Croatian population to a policy that had no foundation or a chance at being implemented, and I believe that for -- you are trying to impute that 16.000 Croats tried to drive out 200.000 Bosnian Muslims, and I think that it just makes no sense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My last question to you is: Was this the same situation that predominated in Vares? Could you make Vares an any more purely Croat area than you could make Kakanj, in your opinion, knowing the area and knowing your common fate?

utterances.speaker: Here we have in front of us a decision from
utterances.text: The time line went as it did, seven days before we -- before us, that Travnik fell or as Muslims prefer to call it, it was liberated. It was Kakanj's turn and Vares remained. And the Doboj county and Tuzla county which used to have 150.000 Croats now is reduced to 19.000 Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But my specific question was Vares faced the same predicament as Kakanj, is that correct? Just a yes or no, and that's the end of it.

utterances.speaker: Here we have in front of us a decision from
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you Your Honours. I shall try to be very brief, only a few questions and it will be the end. Re-examined by Mr. Naumovski:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Towards the end of cross-examination, you were asked a number of questions, why did all the HVO leaders leave Kakanj, and you said, you said about your yourself, "I did not leave, I was expelled." Now, what was it that you said that forced all the Croats headed by their leadership to leave Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: Here we have in front of us a decision from
utterances.text: They were forced by hundreds of rifles pointed at the Croat people, and the Croat Defence Council. They were forced by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina with all the fate-forcing units which were attacking the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. The document Z1110, and the list, it was said, incidentally, that the document does not use the word expellee but refugee. In the Croatian version, it said, "People expelled from the area of Kakanj." Under 112, it says, "Pavo Sljivic and his family." Would you please repeat it because it conspires from this document that from Kakanj you went to Kiseljak in June 1993?

utterances.speaker: Here we have in front of us a decision from
utterances.text: No, I have already said it two or three times that from Kakanj, I left on foot to Vares through the woods, and from there, on the 17th of October, 1993, I headed from Vares to Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And those are thousands of expellees which had to go from Kakanj to Vares in June 1993. Did they have to go through Serb territories held by the army of Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: Here we have in front of us a decision from
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As for that meeting in Kakanj of Z29 [sic] held of the 30th of September. There were very many questions about it; I have only one. Are you sure -- it's "229", not "Z29", but "Z229". Just one question, are you sure, Mr. Sljivic, that at that time, only one meeting was held at the time or perhaps were there more meetings? I'm referring to the period around the 30th of September 1992?

utterances.speaker: Here we have in front of us a decision from
utterances.text: I do not know because I simply have not kept all the HVO documentation. I am positive, however, that neither was anybody authorized nor could anyone in my name convene and chair a meeting, not to mention without letting me know about it, and for me to see such a document for the first time here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. A great deal was said about reasons for your substitution by Mr. Pavlovic. Now, as for those suspicions which somehow were attached to your name, was there any investigation conducted?

utterances.speaker: Here we have in front of us a decision from
utterances.text: I asked this August Court to allow me to explain when the Prosecutor pounced upon me trying to mar my reputation as a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. There is no question of your reputation being marred and there's no question of the Prosecutor pouncing upon you. She is entitled to ask questions. She is entitled to put the documents which she put to you. Had that not been the case, we would have stopped her. Let me explain. Your role is that of a witness. Not, if I may say so, to make comments or speeches. Now, you may answer the question that was put to you, but would you restrict yourself to answering it. You were asked whether any investigation was conducted. Now, was there an investigation or not?

utterances.speaker: Here we have in front of us a decision from
utterances.text: There was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever charged of the things that you were suspected of as a result of the investigation?

utterances.speaker: Here we have in front of us a decision from
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, I understood you. But what I was trying to say was: Even in the wake of the war, you still enjoyed the trust of the citizens of Kakanj. You were elected to the municipal council first, and now you're a member of the parliament of the Federation, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: Here we have in front of us a decision from
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Naumovski. You mentioned the trust, the citizens had placed in the witness. In order to be a member of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, do you have to be elected by citizens?

utterances.speaker: Here we have in front of us a decision from
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you have been elected, but which were the people who elected you? Where were you elected as a member of the parliament of the Federation?

utterances.speaker: Here we have in front of us a decision from
utterances.text: In the elections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When was that?

utterances.speaker: Here we have in front of us a decision from
utterances.text: October 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you were elected in what constituency?

utterances.speaker: Here we have in front of us a decision from
utterances.text: I was elected in the general elections so that general to the Federation, all the citizens in all municipalities voted for names on the lists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, you were elected on the basis of a list because your party had put you on a list; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Here we have in front of us a decision from
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you.

utterances.speaker: Here we have in front of us a decision from
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honours, the election of the president, of the mayor, and councilman is not the same. To become a councilman, 80 per cent of the Muslim councilmen would have to vote for me for me to become the mayor, because there were six Croats in the council of the HDZ and two more Croats from opposition parties and all the others were Muslims. And they elected me, the mayor, that is the president of the municipal council unanimously.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was about to ask you a question about this. There was this question about elections, who elected you and so on so forth. Perhaps the court does not know it because we simply did not have the opportunity to ask about that, but Bosnia-Herzegovina is -- stands rather unpowered from other places after Dayton because the manner of elections and voting procedures were regulated by the Dayton. As for the local elections, that is, the election of councilmen in the municipality of Kakanj, will you agree with me that all citizens of Kakanj voted for councilmen in Kakanj regardless of whether they were living in Kakanj or outside Kakanj at the time of the elections?

utterances.speaker: Here we have in front of us a decision from
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And even people were Kakanj who were living in the Netherlands as displaced persons could vote for them?

utterances.speaker: Here we have in front of us a decision from
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is as far as the local elections are concerned, isn't it. And likewise, all those who had the place of residency in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time of war, regardless of where they are now still have their right to vote and be elected; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: Here we have in front of us a decision from
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We also heard Z87. This could be my last question, a document, about your appointment to the Croat Defence Council Kakanj, and those items, one which says that you were selected by Mr. Boban. Although this is the first time you see this document, we can agree that this document is from May 1992, that that was the time when some authorities amongst the Croat in the HVO, that is HZ HB were not yet founded on quite sound foundations. It was May 1992 so the JNA was still in Bosnia-Herzegovina, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: Here we have in front of us a decision from
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this would be the end of my redirect. Thank you very much and thank you, Mr. Sljivic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivic, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, as I understand it, there's an application in respect of the next witness for various matters. Presumably we should go into private session to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I would appreciate it. I would appreciate it, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We have in mind the Trial Chamber's injunction to us that matters such as this should be covered by affidavit and that's why we've done that. This witness was the only witness along the lines of a Croat victim that we presently propose to introduce. We understand that another such witness, the mother of some of the children that were blown up when the shell landed in the playground in Vitez just shortly before the Tuzla convoy has testified in the Blaskic case. I believe the cross-examination of the witness "DQ", I think, the identifier. Some of the cross-examination or all of it took place in closed session. Respectfully, we would like to make an application for the closed session testimony intending to use the transcript of the witness' prior testimony instead of her to come and relive those awful events in the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we will grant leave. Mr. Sayers, while we're -- yes, the next witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, if you'd like to take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Please take a seat. Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Major?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please state your full name for the Court?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: I am Franjo Ljubas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major, I would like to take you briefly through some matters of background. I'll do it very cursorily. I believe you were born on April 5th, 1969 in the town of Travnik?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you completed elementary school in Novi Bila and then graduated from high school in 1988; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Yes. In 1988.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After graduating from school, I believe that you fulfilled your compulsory national service in the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA for about a year, and then following the completion of that service in 1989 returned to your home town of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and a Croat by ethnicity, and a Roman Catholic by religion; is that correct, Major?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe that in 1990, you became a member of the principal Bosnian Croat political party, the Croat Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you know that a referendum was held on the independence of your country, sir, on February the 29th and March the 1st of 1992. How did you vote?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Yes, I know I voted for an independent and integral Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, did your fellow Croats overwhelmingly do the same thing as did you, vote in favour of the independence of their country?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Yes, and the results of the elections showed that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are currently enrolled, sir, I believe, at Teachers' Training College in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is it that you are undertaking training to teach, Major?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: I'm studying Croatian language and literature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And I believe that you were also working in the headquarters of the 3rd Division of the 1st Guard Corps of the Army of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, stationed in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm an officer in the Federation army, and I am a mayor [as interpreted], my rank is mayor [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that "major"?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It is, excuse me. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're married, and you have one child, I believe.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm married and have one child.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to address your attention, Major, to the summer of 1991, when hostile activities were initiated against the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Slovenia by the former JNA. Could you tell the Court what your involvement was in activities following those attacks? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Yes. When the JNA aggression against the Republics of Slovenia and Croatia started, we, the Croats in the municipality of Travnik and all the other places, realised that an aggression against the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina would follow. And in the light of that, we tried to organise the defence, and we undertook preparations to set up war staffs because it had transpired that the JNA was pulling out equipment and armament from the municipality of Travnik and other places and replacing them, and also men whom they were concentrating on Mount Vlasic. And it was therefore clear that aggression was looming ahead and we had to do something in order to organise ourselves and put an end to the aggression, if it took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What exactly did you do, Major, in connection with making these military preparations?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: As for the military preparations, we tried to collect weapons on a voluntary basis first, and then we also trained individuals who would volunteer to protect the Lasva Valley, Travnik, and all the population in the area. And we supported the organisation of municipal war staffs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did there come a time when you participated in the formation of the Sveti Duh Company in Nova Bila?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Yes. To prevent the Yugoslav People's Army to pull out the armament from Bratstvo and other military facilities and barracks in the Lasva area, on the 27th of February -- one of such gatherings to prevent the pullout of this weaponry was the 27th, when the JNA tried to pull out some of the armament and material from the Bratstvo compound. At the same time, the JNA was bringing some forces from the area of Vlasic towards Travnik. And if I may add --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't mean to be discourteous, but the Court has already heard a lot of evidence about what happened in the early days in the Travnik area. I just wanted you to tell the Court about the part that you took in the formation of the Sveti Duh Company and what the significance of that company was for later military organisations in the Travnik area, in a few words.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Yes. So on the 27th, we met and set up a unit and called it Company Sveti Duh, Holy Spirit, and I was in the command of that unit which was made of volunteers. It lasted until the HVO was founded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And the Court knows that the Croat Defence Council was formed on April the 8th, 1992. When it was formed, sir, did you join it, and if so, what was the position to which you were appointed?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Yes. When the HVO was formed on April the 8th, 1992, I was appointed the commander of the 4th Company in Nova Bila, and I kept that post until sometime in July 1992. After that, I became deputy commander of the 2nd Battalion of the Municipal Headquarters, Travnik, until sometime in September of 1992. And after that, I was posted the commander of the 3rd Battalion of the Travnik Brigade until the 13th of June, 1996, when I was -- 1993, when I was wounded while exercising that duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you referred to appointment to the position of a company commander, commanding the 4th Company of what battalion?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: At that time, it was the 2nd Battalion, that is, the 2nd Battalion. In September, it was renamed, the same unit, and became the 3rd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, sir. I believe that your battalion, the 3rd Battalion of the Travnicka Brigade, on April the 1st, 1993, was split into two, and that three quarters of the brigade was reformed into the Frankopan Brigade, while the remaining one quarter, including yourself, stayed in the 3rd Battalion of the Travnicka Brigade thence forward. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's accurate to say that the commander of the Frankopan Brigade, after it was formed on April the 1st, 1993, was a man named Ilija Nakic?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While your brigade commander, the commander of the Travnicka Brigade, was Jozo Leuter?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it accurate, sir, that commanders of both the Frankopan and the Travnicka Brigades took their orders directly from their superior officer?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I could fathom the chain of command, they were the ones who received orders through the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was their superior officer?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Well, I told you. As far as I knew about the chain of command, they were receiving orders from the then Colonel Tihomir Blaskic, and Colonel Blaskic was then receiving orders from the head of the Main Staff in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You made a brief reference, Major, to the fact that you were wounded in June of 1993?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was in the village of Dolac, I believe, during the ABiH offensive.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were treated in the hospital in Nova Bila, where you stayed until September of 1993?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this hospital facility located in a converted church?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it marked in any fashion, Major, to alert people that in fact it was a hospital facility, providing services for people who had been wounded or sick?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I know it was marked, because that hospital was founded at that time when, from the Travnik hospital -- that is, it was one of those incidents which happened when 110 HVO wounded were thrown out of that hospital. So they were put at that particular place, and the red cross was painted on the roof to mark it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: At that time when the hospital was established, it was my area of responsibility. So the order came from me, in agreement, because it was the only place in that area. So I agreed about that with the parish priest, the one who was in that church, to put up the wounded there. And they ordered my subordinates to mark it and secure it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the red cross was placed on the roof of the church, sir, do you know whether this church had been shelled by ABiH forces at all?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Well, what is evident is that the church was shelled. It was shelled on the eve of the biggest ABiH offensive, in the course of the biggest offensive, and until the end of the conflict -- rather, the conclusion of the ceasefire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying that the shelling of this converted church, now hospital facility, continued notwithstanding the painting of the red cross on the roof of the church?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Yes, and I think that to this day the church was not completed, and I believe I could go back and see traces of mortar shells on the church itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one final question on this subject, sir, since it has received some attention during the evidence. Could you just describe, in your own words, the kinds of conditions in which the wounded people or sick people at this hospital facility were actually kept?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Well, I can describe the area that was used for their accommodation. There was a large number of wounded, so it was the room where mass was celebrated, and there were benches for the congregation. So those benches were simply put together, and then we used the sponges in order to improvise some mattresses. And it was on those makeshift cots that the worst cases could lie, and others were simply put up in houses nearby. I was accommodated in one of them after I was wounded. That is, I was first hospitalised, and then I was taken to one of the houses near the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Just moving forward in time, sir. After you were released from the hospital in approximately October of 1993, you were assigned to the command or the headquarters of the Travnicka Brigade as an officer; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Yes. After my treatment, I was assigned to the command of the Travnik Brigade, which was October 1992 -- sorry, 1993, and that is where I was until January 1994, when I was transferred to the newly-formed 3rd Guards Brigade, and that is where I was until June 1999.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just going back in time, Major Ljubas, if I may -- and this is at paragraph 12 of the outline, Your Honours -- after the Bosnian Serb army and JNA had attacked your country in March and April of 1992, you've already described that efforts were made to organise yourselves into an armed force in the municipalities. Could you tell the Court, in these extremely early days of the conflict, March, April, May, even June of 1992, were the civilian and military authorities all jumbled together or did the two exist separate and independent of one another? Of the HVO, I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: As for the civilian and the military part, they were two separate things and each had its own field of jurisdiction. The military part had a lot of work to do to establish the front line and stop or forestall the offensive against the area, because the JNA had blocked the principal routes needed for the supply of food, medicines, and other basic necessities. The civilian part of the HVO took care of these latter aspects, that is, provision of food, medicines and the rest for the civilian population. For example, the principal road coming from south, that is, from maritime ports, and then on from Kupres, Gornji Vakuf, Travnik, and so on and so on, this road was blocked, so that the only access road was the Makadam road coming from Novi Travnik towards Uskoplje and then on to Herzegovina. This was the Makadam road. I emphasise this point. And the civilian wing of the HVO at that time already was trying to put it in proper order and use it for the supply of food and medicines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was the civilian component of the HVO responsible for the procurement of food, logistic supplies, for the civilian population as well as the military, or not?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Well, the civilian wing had to take care of food and medicines as a whole, because the members themselves were individual civilians from that area, who lived there, whose family members were in that area for which the civilian HVO was providing with food and medicines. Of course, it was for them too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've just described the Makadam road that leads north from Uskoplje to the Novi Travnik area. This road had been built when, or was it completed?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: That road was not completed. It -- in 1991, the civilian wing tried to get some machinery from the Sebes company in Nova Bila and tried to use that machinery in order to make the route possible and usable for the food and medicines. We tried to arrive at an agreement, at an understanding, with Muslims. At first, they refused to take part in the construction of that road, so we had to invest our utmost effort. That is, the civilian part had -- the civilian wing had to do it in order to make that road usable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, in terms of morale, weapons and equipment, could you just give the Court your assessment of how the ABiH was situated, vis-a-vis the HVO, to deal with the Serb offensives, the Bosnian Serb army offensives with which it was confronted in March, April and May of 1992, sir?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, the HVO was, in morale terms, well prepared, but had inadequate armament and material. And in spite of that lack of armament and material, the HVO succeeded in bringing to a halt the major part of the JNA offensive, as demonstrated by the fact that the HVO kept about 30 per cent of the territory in the offensive, whereas the Muslims or, rather, the ABiH, as it later became, were not ready, were not prepared to resist the JNA offensive, because at that time the thesis that circulated amongst the Muslims was that it wasn't their war. But the fact is, that in those early days of the offensive in Travnik, where I was, the HVO had established almost two thirds of the front line, that is, where it stopped the JNA, subsequently called the army of Republika Srpska. We managed to stop them there, and the Muslims, and later on members of the ABiH, held less than one third of the whole front line in the municipality of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Major, the suggestion has been made in this case that by October of 1992, the HVO had actually abandoned the front lines with the BSA at Jajce and the environs of Travnik and Turbe. Is that accurate, or could you give the Court some help on whether that's an accurate assessment or not?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry if my question was elliptical. A suggestion has been made in this case that the HVO abandoned the front lines at Jajce and in the areas around Jajce in October of 1992. Is that accurate or not?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: It is not accurate. In October '92, the HVO still held the front in Travnik. It is true that in October '92, the front in Jajce fell, held by both HVO and the BH army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A suggestion -- there are two other suggestions that have been made, Major. The first is that actually it was the ABiH that was providing the vast majority of the armed forces on the front lines at Jajce. Could you give the Court your assessment of the accuracy of that position, please?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: That is not true. As far as I know and as far as I sent my forces to the front -- to the Jajce front, that is not true. The major part of the front in Jajce was held -- was manned by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And then the final suggestion along these lines is that the HVO voluntarily withdrew from Jajce, pursuant to an agreement with the Bosnian Serb army, rather than suffering a military defeat that resulted in the capture of that town, as you've just related. Which version is accurate, Major, according to your own personal experience?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: It is not true that the HVO withdrew of its own will. At some point, BH army forces began to retreat from the front line in Jajce, and the army of Bosnian Serbs sensed that, and in a forceful assault, managed to break through the front and expel all the population of the area of Jajce in the direction of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, thank you, Major. The Court has already heard evidence about the large number of Bosnian Muslim refugees that resulted from the BSA and JNA offensives to the north-east and north-west of the country and also the influx of refugees as a result of the fall of Jajce. Could you give the Court a feel for what was done to accommodate these unfortunate displaced people, these people who had been expelled from their homes?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: At that time, the JNA, that is the Bosnian Serbs, expelled to the area of Travnik and it had at least 50.000 inhabitants, mostly Muslims from Kotor Varos and Jajce. There were some Croats there too, and the HVO at that time, in order to assist with the accommodation of all these displaced persons, offered the Travnik barracks which it shared with the ABiH. That was the Travnik barracks which were shared 50/50 between the HVO and the ABiH. And later on, the ABiH abused this and it accommodated the 17th Krajina Brigade there later on. And we also placed both Muslims and Croat refugees in school buildings in, for instance, in the areas like Novi Bila, Dolac, Guca Gora where Croats were in majority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was talking in general terms still. Could you give the Court an assessment of how the ABiH fared in organisational terms with the HVO as 1992 wound on into 1993?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Regarding 1992, I have already said that ABiH, until October 1992, ABiH was poorly organised and unprepared for defence. But in October 1992 after the fall of Jajce and part of the Kotor Varos municipality, ABiH started receiving weapons and equipment. The 1st and the 7th Krajina Brigades led by Alagic and Cuskic arrived from Croatia, and they were well-equipped and well-armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to interrupt you if I may, you say that General Alagic and Fikret Cuskic arrived with the 7th Krajiska Brigade and the 1st Krajiska Brigade?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: The 1st and the 7th which was later merged into the 17th Krajina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are these units forces which were originally amassed and organised in the neighbouring Republic of Croatia. Correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Yes. And they arrived in the Travnik area and were billeted in the Travnik barracks which originally the HVO had vacated in order to accommodate -- to have the refugees accommodated there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you were saying in connection with the relative degrees of organisation, in the ABiH as opposed to the HVO, you had reached October of 1992. Could you give your views about how the organisational competencies of the HVO and ABiH compared after that date, sir?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: After October, 1992, the demographic breakdown of the area changed. There was a large influx of civilian and militarily-fit population so that the Muslim population became much more numerous than the Croatian population in that area. And also at that time, there was an influx of armaments and equipment, and the ABiH had a plan in -- of bringing in weapons and organising troops there. Starting in October, 1992, also groups of Mujahedin appeared who were previously not seen in that area. There were --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll get to that shortly, but let me just ask you a couple of simple questions. By June of 1993, in your military assessment, what was the ratio of ABiH armed forces to HVO armed forces in terms of manpower?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: At the time in June of 1993, there were -- the ratio was about eight Muslim soldiers to one HVO soldier. In other words, a far superior force of ABiH in relation to HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And in terms of military equipment, how did the ABiH fare vis-a-vis the HVO in your military opinion?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Regarding the military equipment, they had four to five times more weapons and equipment than what the HVO had at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Just one digression, if I may, regarding the accused in this case, Mr. Dario Kordic. What did you know about him while you were an officer in the HVO, Major?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Mr. Dario Kordic was an active politician. He had nothing to do with the military side of the HVO, specifically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you know, did he have the power, ability, authority, however you want to phrase it, to issue orders to any military units of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: As far as I know, and I emphasize that, Mr. Kordic was not part of the military chain of command and he, in particular, never issued any orders to me or to any of my subordinates. Had he done so, I would not have carried it out because I had my own chain of command. Neither I would have, nor any of my subordinates would have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Major, let's just move on. You, before I interrupted you, I hope not rudely, you were just talking about the military build-up in the area of Travnik on the part of the ABiH armed forces, but let's go back to 1992, specifically to October 20th, 1992. There was then, I believe, an instant involving Ivica Stojak. Could you just tell the Court who he was and what happened on that date?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: On the 20th of October 1992, the commander of the Travnik headquarters was killed. The -- it was a result of an attack by the Mujahedin and the Muslim forces near Medresa where a checkpoint was set up and where they wait for a commander of the municipal headquarters and they killed him there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what can you tell us about Mr. Stojak? Did he ever advocate bad relations with the Muslims or violence against them?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Ivica Stojak, as a commander of the municipal headquarters, was the highest authority, both among the Croats and Muslims. This was a person who, as commander of the municipal headquarters, did a lot to stop the advance of the Bosnian Serb army and who maintained good relations between the Croats and Muslims in this municipality. A person who tried to involve the Muslims and the ABiH in all operations which were jointly carried out. For instance, the take over of the Slimena barracks and the Travnik barracks were alongside the ABiH. The barracks was taken and the facility was split between the two sides in equal parts. And he -- and a commander, and a Croat was appointed commander and his deputy a Muslim. So he was a person who helped both Croats and Muslims who could not find ways to resolve their problems; health problems, social problems, so maintained good relations in the entire municipality and precisely because of the person he was, the Muslims killed him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe, sir, that in your area, there were a number of incidents in 1992 and 1993 which caused tensions between the ABiH and HVO to riot. Could you just tell the Court a little bit about those in your own words.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: I have pointed out that the erosion of this good relations started with the arrival of Mehmed Alagic and Fikret Cuskic and that is after the fall of Jajce and the arrival of Mujahedin. And also the murder of the commander of municipal headquarters contributed to that. Other incidents followed and all against the HVO. So these incidents started as early as January and it continued until June when the open offensive took place, and I can cite a number of examples.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's try to take it step by step, Major. In March of 1993, on March 17th to be specific, was there an incident that occurred fairly close to your command post.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Yes. Some 500 metres from where I was at an intersection near the intersection of Dolac, a group of Mujahedin and ABiH soldiers shot and killed two HVO members shooting from a van. The soldiers killed were Ivo Juric and Zoran Matosevic. Both members of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About three or four weeks after that, was there an incident of an arrest of two prominent Croats in your town and, if so, could you tell the Court a little bit about that?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Yes, this happened around April 9. Prominent Croats were arrested in the town of Travnik itself. I can mention some of their names. One of them was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- about how many of these were --

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Yes. So prominent Croats who were detained and taken to the fort who later became one of the ABiH camps. This was in the old part of town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About how many such people were there who had been arrested?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: At first, about 70 Croats were arrested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it the case that these people were released only to be re-arrested?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Yes. At first, they were released and later on, they were arrested again and some of them were taken, some stayed behind, but some were taken to Mehurici, to another of their camps, where they were mistreated by the members of ABiH.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Major. The Court has already heard about the incidents of around Easter of 1993 during which some Croat flags were torn down and burned and there was a brief bit of fighting in the town. If you were asked questions about that, you could answer them, I take it?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you also describe for the Court whether any injured or wounded HVO soldiers were evicted from the Travnik hospital in mid-April of 1993 and, if so, under what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Yes. In mid-April, about 110 wounded HVO members were evicted from the hospital in Travnik. This hospital which was a general hospital used by all the people of Travnik. They were transferred to a church in Novi Bila which was turned into a make-shift hospital. This was another incident provoked by ABiH members, so these incidents ranged from flag burning to murders. And I can say that I was stopped and disarmed, both myself and my driver and my escort. We were all disarmed and I reported to -- I informed the commander at Plave Vode and asked if, that my weapons be returned. He just laughed and refused to return it to me. That was just another incident. So later on my driver and some other officers were again stopped in the town in their vehicle and they were beaten up on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you know that there was a very serious outbreak of fighting in the Vitez area in April of 1993. During that fighting, where were you stationed?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: At that time, I was with the part of my units on the front line against the BSA forces, so my -- as part of my units were deployed in the area of Kajabasa-Krizi and the area of Mescema near Turbe. In other words, I was on the front line against the army of Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You did hear, I believe, about an incident that occurred in late April of 1993 involving 50 or so soldiers from the 7th Muslim Brigade who attacked or rounded up the civilians in the village of Miletici moving about 30 or so of them or so to the neighbouring village of Poljanice, and executing five people from the Pavlovic or Petrovic family. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: This was the Pavlovic family. I am familiar with these incidents where Mujahedin and members of the 7th Muslim Brigade took people from -- to the village of Poljanice near Mehurici. They were civilians and they were released a couple of days later. When the civilians came back to the village they found five civilians, that is, five members of the Pavlovic family killed, murdered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Moving on to just shortly before the ABiH offensive, could you tell the Court about what happened to Croat civilians in the village of Polje in early June of 1993, Major?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: In early June or more specifically on 3rd June, ABiH stepped-up the incidents and sniping from the surrounding areas of Slimena, Vakuf which were around the village of Polje. This is when the first Croats were killed in that area. In the span of time between the 3rd and the 6th, a total of 12 Croats were killed in the village of Polje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Major. Let me just ask you a general question now for the Court's information, this is paragraph 25 and 26 of the outline, and I'll try to move through this quickly. Did you notice, before the initiation of the June 1993 ABiH offensive, any troop build-ups in the -- in your area of operations?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Yes. In the period between April and June, I observed that the ABiH was bringing in large forces from Zenica area, from Guca Gora, and on the way back, we noticed that the -- the buses were empty which was different. Until then if they came this way full, then they would also return full. But this time around, full buses were going one way and empty buses were returning to Zenica. They were not being deployed on the front line against the Bosnian Serbs, that for us, was a signal that the ABiH was preparing something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By June of 1993, Major, what kind of forces had the ABiH managed to amass in the Travnik area?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: By early June, the 17th Krajina Brigade was there, was deployed, parts of 7th Muslim Brigade. Then the local brigades, the 306th and 312th Brigades and then the 305th Jajce Brigade which had been expelled from Jajce and part of Kotor Varos municipalities. Then the 27th and 37th Brigades which were deployed there, brought there and the Mujahedin were deployed alongside the 7th Muslim Brigade. And looking at these forces in total, the -- up to 10.000 troops were brought to that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Was the 308th Brigade there or not, or units of the 308th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Yes. These were parts of the 308th Brigade up to a force of about one battalion strength.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these significant forces were commanded by whom, sir?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: These forces were commanded by Mehmed Alagic and they were part of the Bosanska Krajina group of which he was the commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was the name of the operative group of the ABiH, the Bosanska Krajina Brigade?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Yes, operative group was called Bosanska Krajina, and General Alagic was its commander and all of the troops of the units that I have mentioned were subordinated to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one small matter of organisational detail that might help the Court. In terms of military organisations, sir, the ABiH, I believe, was organised into these operative groups which would be in -- the functional equivalent for the HVO would be an Operative Zone. Is that fair to say or is it not?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's probably a hopeless question. In terms of the organisation of the ABiH, sir, the ABiH was organised into broad areas called operative groups was that the functional equivalent in the HVO's military organisation, the so-called Operative Zone such as the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, for example?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: In that area, there was one Operative Zone. It was the Central Bosnia Operative Zone and subordinated to this zone were brigades.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the organisational structure used by the ABiH was to use an operative group which contained brigades as well. Is that accurate to say or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it that you know or you don't know, sir?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO LJUBAS
utterances.text: I just said so. The area under the control of the HVO was called the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, and it had under it brigades where as the ABiH had an operative group commanded by General Alagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: 15 minutes tomorrow, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, well it would be a convenient moment. It may be convenient if we deal with the affidavit on Friday and we also deal with the issue of the exhibits at the same time. Mr. Sayers, I'm going to ask you something which would be helpful to the Court and that is to produce a schedule or a list of your affidavits. There now must be 12 or 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: 12 to date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you could list them for us in some convenient way so that we have them in front of us, give them numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So we can use this during -- in case there's any questions of admissibility and also, it would be helpful if we could have a brief summary of topics they deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, that should be possible and I'll try to bring it along tomorrow morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: By Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Major Ljubas, we're adjourning now until tomorrow morning. Will you be back please at half past nine to continue with your evidence. Would you remember during the adjournment not to speak to anybody about your evidence, please, until it's over and of course don't let anybody speak to you about it. That does include members of the Defence team. Half past nine tomorrow, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: at 4.03 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday the 17th day of May 2000, at 9.30 a.m. 24 25
